title: Hybrid life cycles
blurb: Explain what a hybrid life cycle combines, the common patterns, when it is applicable and what it takes to make it work.
question: A rail operator is upgrading a station. The new ticket gates must be installed to a safety-approved design, but the passenger app that works with them will be shaped by commuters' feedback. The project manager proposes one project using two approaches. What is this called, why does it suit the project, and what must be managed carefully?

teach.h: Use each approach where it fits
teach.body: A hybrid life cycle combines linear and iterative approaches within the same project, using each for the parts of the work it suits best. In plain English: plan and gate the parts that are fixed, regulated or physical, and iterate the parts where needs are uncertain and feedback adds value. It is a deliberate design decision made at the start, not a mixture that happens by accident.

teach.h: Northgate station upgrade: one project, two approaches
teach.caption: Each part is matched to the approach its certainty, regulation and need for feedback call for.

teach.h: Pattern 1: linear front end, iterative build
teach.caption: Common where a board wants formal approval and a fixed budget before work starts, but the detail is best discovered with users.
The two workstreams run side by side and must come together for integration and handover.

teach.body: Real projects rarely have one level of certainty throughout. Hybrid is applicable when different parts have different levels of certainty or risk, when governance or regulation demands gates and approvals but users still need to shape the solution, or when the organisation wants a controlled, fully approved investment that still delivers some value early. It aims to get the control and predictability of linear where they matter and the flexibility and feedback of iterative where they matter.

teach.caption: Whatever the mix, there is still one business case and one sponsor for the whole project.

teach.h: Making hybrid work: interfaces and governance
teach.body: The hard part is where the approaches meet. At Northgate, the app's third time box needs the gates installed to test against; if the gate work slips, the app team stalls. So the project needs one governance framework that respects gates and time boxes, clear dependencies and integration points, roles that fit both (a project manager and a product owner who work together), and reporting that turns time-box progress into the overall plan. The rationale for each part's approach is recorded in the project management plan.

teach.h: Linear, iterative and hybrid side by side

teach.text: Hybrid is NOT switching between approaches whenever pressure builds, with no rationale. That causes confusion and loss of control. It is a planned combination, with each part's approach decided up front and one aligned governance framework. Also don't confuse hybrid (mixing linear and iterative) with the EXTENDED life cycle (adding Adoption and Benefits realisation after Transition).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define it: a planned combination of linear and iterative approaches in one project.
Say when it fits: parts with different certainty, regulation alongside uncertain user needs.
Give the benefit: control and predictability where needed, flexibility and feedback elsewhere.
Give the limitation: complexity at the interfaces; governance and reporting must be aligned.
Link to the scenario: say which part would be linear, which iterative, and why.
Hybrid combines linear and iterative approaches within one project.
Common patterns: linear front end with iterative build, or parallel linear and iterative workstreams.
Applicable when certainty, risk or regulation differ across parts of the work.
It needs one aligned governance framework and careful management of interfaces.
Ad hoc switching is not hybrid; hybrid is not the extended life cycle.

summary: You can now explain what a hybrid life cycle combines, describe the two common patterns and say when hybrid is applicable. You can also explain why the interfaces and governance between the linear and iterative parts must be carefully aligned.

A.q: Which best describes a hybrid life cycle?
options: A linear life cycle plus benefits phases
Iterative cycles with no defined phases
Linear and iterative used in one project
Changing method whenever the team likes
A.why: A hybrid life cycle deliberately combines linear and iterative approaches within the same project.

whyNot.0: Adding Adoption and Benefits realisation describes the extended life cycle.
whyNot.1: Iterative cycles alone are an iterative life cycle, and it still has defined phases.
whyNot.3: Changing method at will is unplanned and causes loss of control; hybrid is a deliberate design.

A.q: Which situation most strongly supports a hybrid life cycle?
options: Some parts are fixed, others uncertain
Every requirement is fixed and agreed
Every requirement is likely to change
The team only knows one way of working
A.why: Mixed certainty across the work is the main reason to combine approaches: linear for the fixed parts, iterative for the uncertain ones.

whyNot.1: If everything is fixed and agreed, a linear life cycle fits the whole project.
whyNot.2: If everything is uncertain, an iterative life cycle fits the whole project.
whyNot.3: Team habit alone is not a reason to choose hybrid; it would argue against it.

A.q: What is usually the key challenge of using a hybrid life cycle?
options: Fixing the scope of every workstream
Delivering any value before the end
A.why: The difficulty lies where the approaches meet: aligning gates with time boxes, managing dependencies and reporting coherently.

whyNot.0: Hybrid deliberately lets scope flex in the iterative parts.
whyNot.1: Fortnightly gates would be an odd design; time-box reviews happen often, gates less so.
whyNot.2: Iterative parts of a hybrid can deliver value early; this isn't its main challenge.

B.q: A bank is replacing branch counters to a fixed, approved design and building a staff app whose screens will be shaped by tellers' feedback. Which approach fits best?
B.why: The counters are physical and fixed, so linear; the app's needs will emerge from tellers' feedback, so iterative.

whyNot.0: This is the wrong way round: physical, fixed work suits linear and evolving software suits iterative.
whyNot.2: Forcing the app into a linear plan loses the feedback the tellers need to give.
whyNot.3: Iterating the physical counters risks costly rework on a fixed, approved design.

B.q: Which element would a hybrid project typically take from the iterative approach?
B.why: Time boxes are an iterative feature that hybrid projects use for the uncertain parts of the work.

whyNot.0: Phase-end decision gates come from the linear approach.
whyNot.1: An up-front fixed design is a linear feature.
whyNot.2: A single handover at the end is linear; iterative delivers in increments.

B.q: Which is the BEST way to reduce the risk of confusion on a hybrid project?
options: Let each team report its own way
Drop the gates once iteration starts
Keep the two streams fully apart
B.why: A single, aligned governance framework gives everyone the same decision points, reporting and escalation routes.

whyNot.1: Separate reporting styles make it hard for the sponsor to see the whole picture.
whyNot.2: Dropping gates removes the control that was the reason for using linear on some parts.
whyNot.3: The streams depend on each other; keeping them apart hides integration risks.

C.q: Northgate's app team finishes time box 3, but the ticket gates it must test against are a month late. What does this illustrate?
options: The app should now switch to linear
Hybrid projects don't need a schedule
C.why: The two workstreams depend on each other. Managing those interfaces and dependencies is the critical discipline in a hybrid project.

whyNot.0: Iterative work can depend on other work, as this case shows.
whyNot.1: Switching the app to linear wouldn't make the gates arrive sooner.
whyNot.3: Hybrid projects need an integrated schedule precisely because the streams interact.

C.q:
Which TWO are benefits of a hybrid life cycle?
1) Control where certainty and regulation demand it
2) No need to plan integration between parts
3) Flexibility where requirements are uncertain
4) A single fixed scope for all the work
C.why: Hybrid gives linear control where it matters and iterative flexibility where it matters.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: integration must be planned carefully in a hybrid project.
whyNot.2: Both are false: integration needs planning, and scope flexes in the iterative parts.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: a single fixed scope would remove the iterative flexibility.

C.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager keeps swapping between linear and iterative working depending on daily pressures, with no recorded reason. Which statement is correct?
options: This is hybrid working at its best
This improves control of the work
This is not planned hybrid working
C.why: A hybrid life cycle is a deliberate design with each part's approach decided and recorded. Ad hoc switching causes confusion and loss of control.

whyNot.0: Unplanned switching is the opposite of a well-designed hybrid.
whyNot.1: Constant switching undermines control; nobody knows which rules apply.
whyNot.2: Reporting becomes harder, not simpler, when the approach keeps changing.

reteach.title: Planning a wedding
reteach.question: A couple books the venue, caterer and date months in advance with signed contracts, but keeps trying out playlists, table plans and decorations with friends right up to the day. How is that a hybrid life cycle?

blocks.h: Fixed where it must be, flexible where it can be
blocks.body: The venue, date and catering are booked early, with deposits, contracts and no room for late change: that is linear. The playlist, the table plan and the decorations are tried, shown to friends and reworked several times: that is iterative. It all comes together on one day, so the couple keeps one master plan and checks that the flexible bits fit the fixed ones (the decorations must suit the venue the couple booked).

blocks.text: The wedding has ONE date and ONE plan. A hybrid project likewise has one business case, one sponsor and one aligned governance framework, even though its parts are run differently.

explain.body: A hybrid life cycle combines the linear and iterative approaches within one project. Each part of the work is matched to the approach that suits its certainty, risk and need for feedback.

test.q: A hybrid life cycle combines which two approaches?
test.why: Hybrid means combining the linear and iterative approaches in one project.

whyNot.1: The extended life cycle adds benefits phases; it isn't what hybrid mixes.
whyNot.2: A product life cycle covers a product's whole life, not a delivery approach mixed in a hybrid.
whyNot.3: Neither of these is a delivery approach that hybrid combines.

explain.body: Concept and Definition run in the linear way, with decision gates, an approved business case and a budget. The build then runs as time boxes with user feedback, and the project finishes with a planned Transition.

test.q: In a hybrid with a linear front end, where does the iterative working usually appear?
test.why: The front end (Concept and Definition) is linear; the build is done in time boxes with user feedback.

whyNot.0: The outline business case is produced in the linear Concept phase.
whyNot.1: Decision gates are a linear control, not iterative working.
whyNot.3: Closure happens in the linear Transition.

explain.body: Different deliverables run side by side, each with its own approach: for example, linear for building works or infrastructure, iterative for software. They meet at planned integration points before handover.

test.q: A hospital is fitting out a new clinic (linear) while developing its booking system with patients (iterative). Which hybrid pattern is this?
test.why: Two deliverables run side by side, each using a different approach: that is the parallel workstreams pattern.

whyNot.0: A linear front end means early phases are linear, then the build iterates; here two streams run in parallel.
whyNot.2: Extended means adding Adoption and Benefits realisation, not mixing approaches.
whyNot.3: The fit-out is linear, so the project isn't purely iterative.

explain.body: Hybrid adds complexity where the approaches meet. It needs one governance framework that respects both gates and time boxes, clear dependencies and integration points, compatible roles, and reporting that rolls time-box progress into the overall plan.

test.q: Why must the governance of a hybrid project be carefully aligned?
options: So scope is fixed in every part
So time boxes can be skipped
So the sponsor is not needed
test.why: Gates and time boxes work at different rhythms; aligned governance makes sure decisions, reporting and escalation work across both.

whyNot.0: Scope flexes in the iterative parts by design.
whyNot.1: Time boxes are how the iterative parts are controlled; they aren't skipped.
whyNot.2: A hybrid project still has one sponsor owning one business case.
